  <h1 class="project-title">Smoke on the water: how wildfire ash affects marine microbial communities</h1>

  <p style="font-size: 14px;  color: #6d6e71; margin-top: 10px;">
  A short reel from a 28 day research cruise off California where we conducted microbial incubation experiments with wildfire ash leachates.
  </p>
</div>

  <p class="project-text">
When wildfire smoke drifts over the ocean, what happens beneath the waves? As climate change alters wildfire activity around the world, understanding how ash deposition influences marine ecosystems is becoming increasingly important.

In a [recent study](https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/lno.70087), we investigated how wildfire ash leachates affect coastal microbial communities along the California coast. Through shipboard incubation experiments, we found that dissolved organic matter (DOM) released from wildfire ash stimulated bacterial growth rates and organic matter remineralization, but did not increase bacterial growth efficiency. This suggests that although bacteria consumed more organic carbon, a greater proportion was not necessarily converted into new bacterial biomass.

We also observed changes in interactions among plankton. Microzooplankton grazing declined while phytoplankton division rates remained relatively stable, suggesting that ash deposition may alter predator–prey relationships and potentially influence phytoplankton accumulation.

Interestingly, the existing biological conditions of the seawater appeared to be more important than differences in ash chemistry in determining how microbial communities responded. In waters with relatively low phytoplankton biomass, bacteria more readily consumed ash-derived DOM. In higher-biomass waters, the added organic matter was less bioavailable, suggesting that the fate of wildfire-derived carbon may depend strongly on the ecosystem receiving it.

We also observed shifts in phytoplankton size structure, with smaller cells becoming more prevalent in high-biomass waters and larger cells increasing in low-biomass waters. Together, these findings suggest that wildfire ash deposition can influence microbial carbon cycling and marine food-web interactions, but that the direction and magnitude of these responses depend on the biological conditions present before deposition.
  </p>
